newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Fired Colombia military head defuses rebellion talk.
newsitem.headline: Fired Colombia military head defuses rebellion talk.

text.p: The dismissed head of Colombia's armed forces defused speculation of a brewing confrontation with President Ernesto Samper on Friday, but hinted he may be preparing a bid for next year's presidential elections.

At a news conference in Quibdo, in northwest Choco province, Gen. Harold Bedoya said Samper's move to fire him on Thursday night -- which cited "reasons of state" -- was an "autonomous decision by the executive."
"My withdrawal was an autonomous decision by the executive...Until the last minute that I was head of the armed forces I sought to fulfil my duty to Colombia," Bedoya told reporters.

In the hours immediately following the announcement of his dismissal, Bedoya said he had not been informed and that he would not resign voluntarily -- fuelling fears he might have been preparing to defy Samper's order.

When asked about speculation that he could launch his candidacy for the 1998 presidential race to replace Samper, he said: "I have said that once I retired and returned to civilian life I would be ready to serve my fellow Colombians in whatever way they considered best."
"As a person with strength and experience, who knows the problems of this country, I'm ready to serve Colombia," Bedoya added.

In recent months, graffiti has been sprayed on walls around Bogota saying "Bedoya for president" "Without Bedoya, down the drain," but it is difficult to determine what real grass-roots support the general's candidacy would receive.

Bedoya has close ties with right-wing factions of the opposition Conservative Party and the ruling Liberal Party. A main plank of any potential election campaign would be his call for a tough line in fighting the country's leftist guerrillas and rejection of peace talks with them.
Foreign Relations Minister Maria Emma Mejia described Samper's surprise dismissal of Bedoya as a clear sign that the armed forces were subject to democratic, civilian rule.
Bedoya's firing took immediate effect but he can officially remain in the army for another three months. He was replaced by the army chief Gen. Manuel Jose Bonett.

At his swearing-in ceremony. Bonett pledged to respect the country's "legally constituted insitutions", adding: "We will search for all means to ensure the tranquility of our country and the free functioning of its institutions."
